title: How to Cope With Layoff Anxiety: 5 Science-Backed Strategies
summary: Layoff anxiety is affecting more workers than ever. Here's why it hits some people harder, and 5 strategies to help you build mental strength.
body_markdown:
## 5 Ways to Cope With Layoff Anxiety


1.


#### Notice and Challenge the Spiral


Not all worry is the same. Some worry leads to a next step, like updating a resume or reviewing a budget. Some worry just replays the same fear over and over, often jumping straight to the worst-case scenario. This idea is central to a[well-studied model](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0145445500245002) for[anxiety treatment](https://lifestance.com/condition-category/anxiety-disorders/) , and a[2023 review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37657623/) found that building tolerance for uncertainty can help ease anxiety symptoms.


The next time worry shows up, try asking yourself: Is there something I can do about this right now? Or am I just rehearsing a fear? If there's a next step, take it. If not, try checking the thought against the facts. What do you actually know right now, versus what you're afraid might happen? This kind of realistic thinking can help build optimism, one of the mental strengths that can buffer against layoff anxiety.


2.


#### Set Boundaries Around Checking and Scanning


Hypervigilance is common with layoff anxiety. This means constantly watching for danger, even when nothing is wrong. It might look like re-reading emails for hidden meaning. It might mean watching a manager's tone for signs of trouble. Or it might mean[doomscrolling](https://lifestance.com/blog/how-to-stop-doomscrolling/) (continuously scrolling on your phone through negative news) about industry layoffs. This can feel protective, but it tends to feed worry instead of solving it. Try setting a specific, limited window for checking news or messages, instead of monitoring constantly. This may help lower the toll it takes, without requiring you to ignore real information.


3.


#### Build a Plan and a Backup Plan


Having a plan can help build hope. Start with a one-page financial snapshot: your savings, your fixed expenses, and how long they'd last without income. Then turn to the professional side: update your resume, refresh your LinkedIn profile, and line up a few references.


It may also help to take stock of your skills, including ones that could transfer to a different role or industry, if needed. The[World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025](https://www.weforum.org/publications/the-future-of-jobs-report-2025/) lists the skills employers need most right now, and expect to need even more by 2030:


- Analytical thinking
- Resilience, flexibility, and agility
- Leadership and social influence
- Creative thinking
- AI and big data
- Networks and cybersecurity
- Technology literacy
- Curiosity and lifelong learning


If any of these feel like a gap, even a small step – like taking a free online course – may help close it. Taking that step can also build efficacy: the confidence that comes from knowing you're equipped to handle whatever is ahead.


4.


#### Protect Your Sense of Self


Job security may start to feel tied to identity and self-worth, especially under the threat of layoffs. But a layoff is almost always a business decision, not a verdict on your skill or effort. Under stress, it can be easy to blur the two, treating the fear of job loss as if it's already a reflection of your worth. Try reminding yourself what's actually true: a layoff would reflect a company's priorities and constraints, not your value as a person.


It may also help to spend time on[relationships](https://lifestance.com/category/relationship-dating/) ,[hobbies](https://lifestance.com/blog/cozy-hobbies-for-mental-health/) , or other roles outside of work. This way, your sense of self doesn't rest on your job alone. Building a fuller life outside of the office can help build resilience: the ability to recover and keep going after something hard happens.


5.


#### Talk About It, and Know When It's Time for More Support


Talking with a trusted friend, partner, or colleague can help ease the feeling of carrying layoff anxiety alone. But sometimes talking to someone you trust isn't enough. Watch for signs like trouble sleeping, trouble focusing, or pulling away from daily tasks or people. If these signs last more than a couple of weeks, that may mean the anxiety has moved beyond everyday stress. A[mental health professional](https://lifestance.com/provider/) can work with you to build tools for managing layoff-related anxiety.[Recent LifeStance data](https://lifestance.com/insight/depression-anxiety-treatment-outcomes/) shows that 79% of LifeStance patients* experienced clinically significant improvement in anxiety symptoms with evidence-based mental health care.
